title: Terror in the Reconstruction South
bigQuestion: How did a secret order use terror to take away freedpeople's rights, and how did witnesses and the law fight back?

story.title: A Long Road to Washington
story.kicker: In 1871, a farmer who lived through a night raid carries his story to Congress.
paragraphs: This scene is a composite. It is built from the kinds of accounts many witnesses gave Congress in 1871. It is spring in upstate South Carolina. A Black farmer stands at the edge of his small cornfield. He is paying for the land, bit by bit. He voted in the last election. Everyone in the county knows it.

A few weeks ago, riders came in the night. Cloth hoods covered their faces. They pulled him from his cabin and whipped him in front of his children. They warned him never to vote again. Before they rode off, he heard one of them laugh. He knew that laugh. It belonged to a man who farms a few miles down the road.

Now word has come that a committee of Congress wants to hear what is happening in the South. He can go and tell his story under oath. His wife is afraid. If the riders learn that he spoke, they may come back. He thinks about it for two nights. Then he packs his one good coat.

In Washington, the room is large and full of strangers. Lawmakers sit at a long table. A clerk writes down every word. The farmer tells what he saw, in order. He names the man he recognized. It is the first time anyone in power has asked him what happened to him.

Across the South, hundreds of people made choices like his. Some spoke when the committee came to their own counties. Others traveled far. Their sworn words filled thousands of printed pages. Those pages are the main reason we know the truth about the first Ku Klux Klan today.
story.think: What risks did witnesses take by testifying, and why do you think so many chose to speak anyway?

lessons.title: After Emancipation
lessons.mainIdea: After the Civil War, new amendments made freedpeople citizens and voters, and many white Southerners were furious.
reading: The Civil War ended in 1865, and about four million enslaved people became free. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified that December, ended slavery in the United States. An *amendment* is a formal change added to the Constitution. Freedpeople moved quickly to build their own lives. They found lost family members, founded churches, opened schools and looked for land and fair pay.

The years from 1865 to 1877 are called *Reconstruction*. During this time the nation rebuilt the South and argued over what freedom would mean. The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made formerly enslaved people citizens. It promised every person equal protection of the laws. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) said no citizen could be denied the vote because of race.

Each *freedperson* now had rights that had been denied for generations. Black men voted in large numbers. Hundreds served in state legislatures, and some went to Congress. Many white Southerners accepted the new order, even if unhappily. Others were furious that Black citizens now shared power. That fury soon took the form of a secret order.

words.d: a formal change added to the Constitution
the years 1865 to 1877, when the nation rebuilt the South and decided what freedom would mean
a person who had been enslaved and was now free

look.title: Three Amendments in Five Years

check.why: The reading says some white Southerners were furious that Black citizens now shared power.

lessons.title: Six Men in Pulaski
lessons.mainIdea: The Ku Klux began in Pulaski, Tennessee, as a club of six Confederate veterans, though its exact founding date is disputed.
reading: Pulaski is a small town in southern Tennessee. There, six young men formed a club they called the Ku Klux. Each was a Confederate *veteran*, someone who had served as a soldier in the war. The traditional founding date is December 24, 1865. The Tennessee Encyclopedia instead places it in May or early June 1866. Historians have not settled which date is right.

The name is usually traced to the Greek word kuklos, meaning circle. The founders borrowed from the lodges of their day. They used grand titles, costumes and an *initiation*, a ceremony for bringing in a new member. At first they rode around town in disguise, playing at mystery. It looked like one more club among many.

Later, the Klan's defenders described this beginning as a harmless joke that got out of hand. Be careful with that story. It came from people who wanted to excuse what followed. A *primary source* is evidence made at the time, like a letter or sworn testimony. The sworn testimony gathered in 1871 shows organized political terror, not a joke.

words.d: a person who has served as a soldier in the armed forces
a ceremony for bringing a new member into a group
evidence made at the time of an event, such as a letter, a photograph or sworn testimony

look.title: Two Founding Dates
look.text: Account A: The club began on Christmas Eve, December 24, 1865. Account B: The Tennessee Encyclopedia says it began in May or early June 1866. Both accounts agree on the town, Pulaski, Tennessee. Both agree that the founders were six Confederate veterans.
look.prompt: Which facts do both accounts share? What kind of primary source would you need to settle the date?

check.q: Where was the Ku Klux founded?
check.why: The reading says six veterans formed the Ku Klux in Pulaski, a small town in southern Tennessee.

check.q: Why should readers be careful with the story that the Klan began as a harmless joke?
choices: It came from a Supreme Court ruling
It was proven by the 1872 report
It was written by the Klan's victims
It came from people who wanted to excuse the violence that followed
check.why: The reading says the joke story came from people who wanted to excuse what followed, while the 1871 testimony shows organized terror.

check.q: What is an initiation?
choices: A ceremony for bringing in a new member
check.why: The reading defines initiation as a ceremony for bringing in a new member, a form the founders borrowed from lodges.

lessons.title: From Club to Terror Network
lessons.mainIdea: By 1868 the Klan had spread across the South as a loose paramilitary network using terror for political goals.
reading: In April 1867, Klan leaders met in Nashville. They adopted a rulebook called the *Prescript*. It set out ranks with grand titles, from local groups called dens up to a Grand Wizard at the top. Historians widely believe the first Grand Wizard was Nathan Bedford Forrest, a former Confederate general. No membership list survives, so the details of his role are still debated.

The Klan spread across the South in 1867 and 1868. Its dens were only loosely connected. Each local group often acted on its own. What joined them was a shared goal. They meant to stop Black citizens from voting, owning land, going to school and holding office. They also meant to drive out white Republicans who worked with them.

Historians call the Klan a *paramilitary* force. It acted like an army without being an official one. Its members used *terrorism*: violence and threats against ordinary people to reach a political goal. Attacks often rose before elections, when votes were at stake. The Klan was no longer a club. It had become a weapon in a fight over who would rule the South.

words.d: the Klan's rulebook, adopted in 1867, which set out its ranks and titles
organized like an army but not an official army
violence and threats against ordinary people to reach a political goal

look.title: Dots on a Map
look.text: Picture a map of the South in 1868 with small dots scattered across it. Each dot is a local den. The lines between the dots are thin and broken. Yet the dots crowd together in places where Black men are about to vote, or where a Black teacher has just opened a school.
look.prompt: What does the pattern of dots suggest about what drove the violence? Why might loose connections make the Klan harder to stop?

check.q: What was the Prescript?
choices: A federal law against the Klan
check.why: The reading says Klan leaders adopted a rulebook called the Prescript in Nashville in April 1867.

choices: It acted like an army without being an official one

choices: Stopping Black citizens from voting, owning land, schooling and holding office
check.why: The reading says the dens were joined by a goal: stopping Black citizens from voting, owning land, going to school and holding office.

lessons.title: Masks and Night Raids
lessons.mainIdea: Klansmen attacked at night in disguise, using violence as intimidation to frighten whole communities.
reading: Klansmen rode at night. They wore robes, hoods or painted masks. They came to a family's cabin in groups. They dragged people outside, whipped them and sometimes killed them. They burned homes, churches and schools. People called these attacks *night riding*.

A *disguise* did two jobs. It hid who the attackers were, so victims could not easily name them in court. It also spread fear. Yet disguises often failed. Survivors frequently knew the riders by their voices, their horses or their size. Many later named these men to Congress. The riders were not strangers. They were local men, and that made the danger closer.

Historians use the word *intimidation* for threats meant to make people too afraid to act. Night riding was intimidation by design. A family whipped for voting was a warning to every family nearby. The goal was not only to hurt one person. It was to make a whole community stay home on election day.

words.d: attacks by groups of disguised men who came at night
clothing or a mask used to hide who a person is
threats meant to make people too afraid to act

look.title: Two Imagined Witnesses
look.text: These two statements are made up for practice. Witness 1: The men wore masks, but I knew one by his voice and his gray horse. He farms the land next to mine. Witness 2: I could not tell who they were. I only know there were many of them, and they came at midnight.
look.prompt: How could each statement help or hurt a case in court? Why might Witness 1 be in more danger after testifying?

check.q: According to the reading, what two jobs did a disguise do?
choices: It kept riders warm and showed their rank
It paid dues and marked members for the army
It impressed judges and hid weapons

check.why: The reading says a disguise hid who the attackers were and also spread fear.

check.q: What is intimidation?
choices: Threats meant to make people too afraid to act
check.why: The reading defines intimidation as threats meant to make people too afraid to act.

check.q: Why was a whipping for voting a warning to every family nearby?
choices: It was listed in the Prescript
The goal was to make a whole community afraid to vote
Neighbors were paid to watch it
check.why: The reading says the goal was to make a whole community stay home on election day.

lessons.title: Who Was Targeted
lessons.mainIdea: The Klan attacked the people who stood for the new South: Black voters, officeholders, teachers, and white Republicans.
reading: The Klan's targets had one thing in common. They stood for the new order in the South. Black voters were attacked. So was any Black *officeholder*, a person elected or appointed to a government job. Black ministers, teachers and families who bought land or asked for fair pay were targeted too. Teachers from the North who taught in freedpeople's schools were threatened.

White Southerners who joined the *Republican* Party were targeted as well. The Klan called them traitors. In the South at this time, a Republican usually meant someone who supported Reconstruction and Black voting rights. The parties have changed a great deal since then. So the word meant something different in 1870 than it does today.

Schools drew special anger. Education let freedpeople read contracts, newspapers and ballots. Many Klan attacks burned schoolhouses or drove teachers away. Yet freedpeople kept rebuilding. Families pooled their money to pay teachers and put up new buildings. Their *persistence*, the act of continuing despite danger, is part of this story too.

words.d: a person elected or appointed to a government job
in the South during Reconstruction, usually a supporter of Reconstruction and Black voting rights
continuing to do something despite danger or difficulty

look.title: A Schoolhouse, Rebuilt
look.text: Picture a one-room schoolhouse in the South in 1870. One night it burns. Within a few months, families have raised money for boards and nails. A new teacher arrives. The children walk to class past the ashes of the old building.
look.prompt: What does the rebuilt school tell you about what freedpeople valued? Why would a group like the Klan see a school as a threat?

check.q: In the South during Reconstruction, a Republican was usually someone who...
choices: supported Reconstruction and Black voting rights
check.why: The reading says a Southern Republican at this time usually supported Reconstruction and Black voting rights.

check.q: Why did schools draw the Klan's anger?
choices: Education let freedpeople read contracts, newspapers and ballots
Schools were owned by the Klan
Schools were used as army forts
check.why: The reading says education let freedpeople read contracts, newspapers and ballots.

check.q: What does persistence mean in the reading?
check.why: The reading defines persistence as the act of continuing despite danger, like families who rebuilt their schools.

lessons.title: Secrecy and the Courts
lessons.mainIdea: Secrecy made Klan terror work because it let members escape local courts, so accountability became the heart of the fight.
reading: Secrecy did more than hide faces. Klan members swore to protect one another. When a case reached a local court, a member might sit on the *jury*, the group of citizens who decide a verdict. Other members could supply an *alibi*, a claim that the accused was somewhere else at the time. Some local sheriffs were members or friends of members.

Witnesses faced a terrible choice. Naming an attacker could bring another raid. Many survivors spoke anyway. Others fled their homes, sometimes hiding in the woods for many nights. Local courts so rarely punished the riders that many Black Southerners came to believe only the federal government could protect them.

Here is the key idea of this chapter. A secret order becomes dangerous when secrecy lets its members escape the law. Many lodges of the time kept harmless secrets, like handshakes and passwords. The Klan used the same forms to hide crimes. That is why *accountability*, making people answer for what they do, became the heart of the fight against it.

words.d: a group of citizens who hear a court case and decide the verdict
a claim that an accused person was somewhere else when a crime happened
making people answer for what they do

look.title: Comparing Two Secrets
look.text: Secret A: A lodge member promises not to tell outsiders the handshake used at meetings. Secret B: A group of men promise not to tell a court who burned a neighbor's house. Both secrets are kept by an oath. Both are kept from outsiders.
look.prompt: What makes Secret A harmless and Secret B a danger to the law? Write one sentence that explains the difference.

check.q: What is an alibi?
choices: A claim that the accused was somewhere else at the time
check.why: The reading defines an alibi as a claim that the accused was somewhere else at the time.

check.q: According to the reading, why did many Black Southerners turn to the federal government?
choices: Local courts rarely punished the riders
Their states had no courts at all
check.why: The reading says local courts so rarely punished the riders that many believed only the federal government could protect them.

check.q: What made the Klan's secrecy different from a typical lodge's?
choices: The Klan used secrecy to hide crimes and escape the law
check.why: The reading says lodges kept harmless secrets, while the Klan used the same forms to hide crimes.

lessons.title: Congress Investigates
lessons.mainIdea: In 1871 a Joint Select Committee of Congress took sworn testimony from hundreds of Southerners and printed it in 13 volumes.
reading: In April 1871, Congress created a *Joint Select Committee*, a special group with members from both the House and the Senate. Its job was to study the condition of affairs in the former Confederate states. In plain words, that meant the violence. Its members heard witnesses in Washington. Some of them also traveled to towns across the South.

Witnesses gave *testimony*, statements made under oath. Clerks wrote down their words. Hundreds of people testified: Black and white, farmers and preachers, officials and Klan suspects. Survivors described raids, whippings and killings. Many named the men they recognized, even though speaking up was dangerous.

The committee sent in its report on February 19, 1872. It filled 13 printed *volumes*, from the Government Printing Office. The first volume holds the report itself. Most of the rest is testimony. Today libraries share these volumes free online. They are one of the richest records of ordinary Americans describing political violence in their own words.

words.d: a special committee with members from both the House and the Senate, formed for one task
a statement made under oath
the separate books that make up one large set

look.title: The Committee's Report
look.text: The committee's report fills 13 volumes. The first volume holds the majority report, the minority's views and the committee's journal of its meetings, from April 1871 to February 1872. The other volumes hold sworn testimony from witnesses about conditions in the Southern states.
look.cite: Joint Select Committee to Inquire into the Condition of Affairs in the Late Insurrectionary States, Report, 13 vols. (Government Printing Office, 1872)
look.prompt: Why might it matter that the majority report, the minority views and the testimony were all printed in the same record?

check.q: What was the Joint Select Committee?
choices: A special group with members from both the House and the Senate
A federal court in South Carolina
check.why: The reading defines the Joint Select Committee as a special group with members from both the House and the Senate.

check.q: How many volumes did the committee's report fill?
check.why: The reading says the report filled 13 printed volumes.

check.q: What is testimony?
check.why: The reading defines testimony as statements made under oath.

lessons.title: Elias Hill of York County
lessons.mainIdea: Elias Hill, a disabled Black preacher and teacher, survived a Klan attack, testified, and led his neighbors to a new life in Liberia.
reading: Elias Hill lived in York County, South Carolina. A childhood illness left him unable to walk or use his arms. He grew up to become a Baptist preacher and a schoolteacher. People in his community trusted him to teach their children to read. They trusted him to lead them in worship.

On the night of May 6, 1871, disguised Klansmen came to his cabin. They dragged him outside and beat him. The attack was aimed at a respected Black leader. When members of the congressional committee came to York County that year, Hill chose to *testify*, or give evidence under oath. He described the attack in careful detail.

Hill was a *witness* and a leader, not someone to pity. After the attack, he decided his community could not be safe at home. In the autumn of 1871 he led a group of neighbors who chose to *emigrate*, or move to another country to live. They sailed to Arthington, Liberia, in West Africa. Hill died there in March 1872. His testimony still speaks for him.

words.d: to give evidence under oath
a person who saw or lived through something and tells about it
to leave your country to live in another one

look.title: A Teacher Gives Evidence
look.text: Picture the scene in York County in 1871. Members of a congressional committee sit at a table. Elias Hill, who cannot walk, has come to speak. A clerk dips his pen. Hill begins to tell, clearly and in order, what happened on the night the riders came.
look.prompt: What kind of courage did it take for Hill to testify? What does his testimony give historians that a newspaper story could not?

check.q: What work did Elias Hill do in his community?
choices: He was a sheriff and judge
He was a Baptist preacher and schoolteacher
He was a member of Congress
check.why: The reading says Hill became a Baptist preacher and a schoolteacher in York County.

check.q: Where did Hill lead a group of neighbors in 1871?
check.why: The reading says Hill led neighbors who emigrated to Arthington, Liberia, in the autumn of 1871.

check.q: According to the reading, how should we see Elias Hill?
choices: As a founder of the Klan
As a witness and a leader
check.why: The reading says Hill was a witness and a leader, not someone to pity.

lessons.title: Two Reports, One Record
lessons.mainIdea: The committee split: the majority found an organized conspiracy, and the minority said the danger was overstated.
reading: The committee did not agree. The Republican members formed the majority. Their *majority report* concluded that the Klan was a real, organized *conspiracy*, a secret plan by a group to do something unlawful. It found that the order used violence to overturn elections and deny citizens their rights. The majority supported strong federal action to stop it.

The Democratic members wrote a *minority report*. They argued that the danger had been overstated. They blamed the Reconstruction state governments for much of the disorder. Both reports were printed together in the first volume. The same testimony stood behind both conclusions.

This gives you a real historian's task. When two groups read the same evidence and reach opposite conclusions, go back to the evidence. Ask who had reasons to see it one way. Each side was *partisan*, strongly loyal to its own party. Historians today, reading the hundreds of sworn accounts, widely agree with the majority on the main point: the Klan was organized terror.

words.d: the conclusions of the larger group of members on a committee
the conclusions of the smaller group of committee members who disagree
a secret plan by a group to do something unlawful
strongly loyal to one political party

look.title: Same Evidence, Two Conclusions
look.text: Majority view, in brief: The attacks follow a pattern. They target voters and officeholders, and the riders act together. This is an organized conspiracy. Minority view, in brief: The disorder is real but exaggerated. It grows out of bad government in the Southern states.
look.prompt: What kind of testimony would you look for to test each view? Which pattern in the evidence would be hardest for the minority view to explain?

check.q: What did the majority report conclude?
choices: The Klan was an organized conspiracy that used violence against citizens' rights
The violence was caused by teachers from the North
The Klan should be made legal
check.why: The reading says the majority found the Klan was a real, organized conspiracy that used violence to deny citizens their rights.

check.q: What is a minority report?
choices: The conclusions of the smaller group of committee members who disagree
check.why: The reading says the Democratic members, the smaller group, wrote a minority report that disagreed with the majority.

check.q: What does partisan mean?
choices: Strongly loyal to one political party
check.why: The reading defines partisan as strongly loyal to one's own party.

lessons.title: The Enforcement Acts
lessons.mainIdea: Congress passed three Enforcement Acts in 1870 and 1871, and part of the Ku Klux Klan Act still protects rights today.
reading: Congress passed three *Enforcement Acts* between May 1870 and April 1871. They were meant to enforce the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments. They made it a *federal* crime to use force or threats to keep citizens from voting. A federal crime is one against the laws of the whole nation. Federal courts, not only local ones, could now hear these cases.

The third law, signed on April 20, 1871, is called the Ku Klux Klan Act. It made it a federal crime to *conspire*, or secretly plan together, to deny people their rights. It also let the president suspend *habeas corpus* where the violence was out of control. Habeas corpus is a person's right to be brought before a judge and not held in jail without cause.

One part of that law still works today. Section 1 lets people sue officials who violate their constitutional rights. It is now known as 42 U.S.C. section 1983. In 1961 the Supreme Court relied on it in Monroe v. Pape, a case about Chicago police who searched a family's home without a warrant. A law written against night riders now protects people across the country.

words.d: three laws of 1870 and 1871 that made it a federal crime to use force to deny citizens their rights
belonging to the national government rather than a state
to secretly plan together to do something unlawful
a person's right to be brought before a judge and not held in jail without cause

look.title: Laws Against the Night Riders
look.cite: U.S. Statutes at Large, vols. 16-17 (16 Stat. 140; 17 Stat. 13); Monroe v. Pape, 365 U.S. 167 (1961)
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Ku Klux Klan Act and Monroe v. Pape? What does that gap tell you about how long a law can matter?

check.why: The reading says the Ku Klux Klan Act let the president suspend habeas corpus where the violence was out of control.

lessons.title: Grant and South Carolina
lessons.mainIdea: President Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties in 1871, leading to arrests and federal trials.
reading: Upstate South Carolina saw some of the worst Klan violence. On October 17, 1871, President Ulysses S. Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine counties there, including York, Spartanburg and Chester. Federal troops and *marshals*, officers who make arrests for the federal courts, moved in. Suspects could now be held for trial without the usual delays.

Hundreds of men were arrested, and many others fled the state. Grant's attorney general, Amos T. Akerman, pushed hard for *prosecution*, the work of bringing criminal charges in court. Federal trials of accused Klansmen were held in South Carolina in 1871 and 1872. Historian Lou Falkner Williams tells their story in a 1996 book.

The trials had real limits. Courts were slow, and only a small share of the accused were ever punished. Still, the arrests broke the Klan's power in much of the South. Survivors had asked for protection, and for a time the federal government answered. It showed that the law could drag a secret order into the open.

words.d: federal officers who make arrests and carry out orders for the federal courts
the work of bringing criminal charges against someone in court
to stop something for a period of time

look.title: Grant's Proclamation
look.text: President Grant declared that unlawful groups in nine South Carolina counties were resisting the laws and the courts could not stop them. He therefore suspended the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus in those counties, so people arrested for these crimes could be held for trial.
look.cite: Ulysses S. Grant, Proclamation 201, Suspending the Writ of Habeas Corpus in Certain Counties of South Carolina, October 17, 1871 (The American Presidency Project)
look.prompt: Grant set aside a basic right in nine counties. What reason does he give? Was the trade-off fair? Explain your answer.

check.q: What did Grant do on October 17, 1871?
choices: He disbanded the Klan in Tennessee
He suspended habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties
He created the Joint Select Committee
check.why: The reading says Grant suspended habeas corpus in nine upstate South Carolina counties on October 17, 1871.

check.q: What is prosecution?
choices: Bringing criminal charges against someone in court
check.why: The reading defines prosecution as the work of bringing criminal charges in court.

check.q: According to the reading, what was one limit of the trials?
choices: The trials were held in Chicago

check.why: The reading says courts were slow and only a small share of the accused were ever punished.

lessons.title: The Order Fades, the Terror Stays
lessons.mainIdea: The first Klan broke up by about 1872, but open groups like the White League carried on its goals and Reconstruction ended in 1877.
reading: By about 1872, the Klan as an organized order had largely broken up. Arrests, trials and federal troops did much of that work. But the Klan's goals did not disappear. *White supremacy*, the belief that white people should rule over others, stayed strong in Southern politics.

New groups took the Klan's place. The *White League*, founded in Louisiana in 1874, did not hide. It operated openly, as an armed force backing the Democratic Party there. In South Carolina, armed men called Red Shirts rode openly during the 1876 campaign. Violence and fraud helped these groups take back state governments.

In 1877 the federal government stopped protecting the last Reconstruction governments, and Reconstruction ended. Over the next decades, Southern states found ways to *disfranchise* most Black men. Remember the witnesses, though. Their testimony became part of the national record. Nearly a century later, the civil rights movement drew on the same amendments and laws they had fought for.

words.d: the false belief that white people should rule over people of other races
an armed group founded in Louisiana in 1874 that used violence openly to end Reconstruction
to take away a person's right to vote

look.title: Masked or Open?
look.text: In 1871, Klansmen rode in masks at night and denied everything in court. In 1874, White League members marched openly in daylight. Both groups used violence to reach the same political goal: ending Black political power in the South.
look.prompt: Why might a violent group stop hiding once it believes no one will stop it? What does this tell you about what the Klan's secrecy was for?

review.q: Why is the Klan's exact founding date still debated?
choices: Different accounts give December 1865 or spring 1866

review.q: Which source holds hundreds of sworn statements from survivors of Klan attacks?

review.q: What did Elias Hill do after surviving the attack on his home?

choices: Hundreds of arrests and federal trials
review.why: The chapter says hundreds of men were arrested and federal trials were held in 1871 and 1872.

review.q: How did the majority and minority reports differ?
choices: The majority found an organized conspiracy; the minority said the danger was overstated
The majority defended the Klan; the minority attacked it
Both said the Klan never existed
Only the minority report was printed
review.why: The Republican majority found an organized conspiracy, while the Democratic minority argued the danger was overstated.

review.q: What made the Klan's secrecy so dangerous?
choices: It let members sell more robes
It let members escape the law
review.why: The chapter's key idea is that a secret order becomes dangerous when secrecy lets its members escape the law.
